title: How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed economists estimate about a quarter of any tariff increase reaches consumer goods prices within a year, roughly two-thirds directly via imports (about 90% import pass-through) and one-third via U.S.-made goods. Tariffs added 2.9 points to goods inflation by Feb 2026; the inflation contribution is forecast to fade toward zero while the price level stays about 2% higher, with Canadian tariffs a renewed source of pressure.

insights.claim: For every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices rise by about a quarter of a percent after one year; a 10 percent tariff on all imports would lift consumer goods prices 2.6 percent after twelve months.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Gives a rule of thumb: roughly 0.25x tariff change to goods CPI, useful for sizing any new tariff shock.
insights.quote: for every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices increase by about a quarter of a percent after one year

insights.claim: Nearly 90 percent of the 2025 tariffs passed through to U.S. import prices, because foreign exporters cut their prices very little; the result holds after controlling for dollar depreciation.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Foreign exporters are not absorbing the tax, so the incidence falls on U.S. importers and consumers rather than on foreign margins.
insights.quote: foreign exporters lowered their prices very little, so that nearly 90 percent of the 2025 tariffs were passed through to U.S. import prices

insights.claim: Retail pass-through from import and producer prices is only about 50 percent, because distribution costs (transport, wholesaling, retailing) are about half of what consumers pay; a 10 percent tariff-driven rise in border/factory prices lifts retail prices 5.6 percent.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Distribution margins dilute tariff shocks at the shelf, so retail inflation understates the import-price hit; this assumes retailers hold margins unchanged in dollar terms.
insights.quote: We find that a 10 percent increase in import and producer prices due to tariffs raises consumer retail prices by 5.6 percent.
insights.locator: Pass-Through from Producer and Import Prices

themes.theme: Hidden indirect effect on U.S.-made goods

insights.claim: Tariffs raise prices of goods not directly taxed: U.S.-made goods account for about a third of the total consumer price effect, via imported inputs (marginal cost channel) and weaker competitive pressure from costlier imports (strategic complementarity).
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Domestic producers gain pricing room under tariffs, so the inflation effect is broader than import-exposed categories.
insights.quote: tariffs also raise the prices of goods that are not directly taxed

insights.claim: The marginal cost channel (tariffs on imported parts and materials, e.g. steel for cars) is larger than the strategic complementarity (markup) channel in the indirect effect.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Input tariffs matter more than markup-taking, so tariffs on intermediates are the key driver of second-round price effects.
insights.quote: the marginal cost effect is the larger of the two

insights.claim: U.S. producer prices respond slowly to tariffs: little in the first six months, then the response roughly doubles over the next six, so the full consumer price effect takes about a year to appear.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Tariff-driven goods inflation lags policy by up to a year, so recent tariff changes keep feeding prices well after they are announced.
insights.quote: The response then builds, roughly doubling over the following six months.

insights.claim: The direct import-price effect reaches consumers fast: about half is in place after three months and all of it by six months, while the indirect effect on retail prices more than doubles between six and twelve months.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Early CPI prints after a tariff change capture mainly the direct piece; the indirect piece arrives later and is stickier.
insights.quote: about half is in place after three months and all of it by six months

insights.claim: The indirect effect is more persistent than the direct effect because U.S. producer prices adjust slowly, so when tariffs are cut the direct effect fades fast but the indirect component lingers.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Tariff rollbacks bring less immediate relief to goods prices than the original imposition caused.
insights.quote: the indirect effect is more persistent because U.S. producer prices adjust slowly
insights.locator: The Tariff Effect on Consumer Goods Inflation Has Peaked

insights.claim: By February 2026 tariffs had contributed 2.9 percentage points to consumer goods price inflation, and without them goods prices would have fallen slightly.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Essentially all of the goods inflation re-acceleration since 2024 is attributed to tariffs, a pointed claim for the goods disinflation narrative.
insights.quote: by February 2026, tariffs had contributed 2.9 percentage points to goods price inflation, and without them goods prices would have fallen slightly
insights.locator: The 2025-26 Tariffs and Consumer Goods Prices

insights.claim: Goods price inflation was near its slightly negative pre-COVID average for most of 2024 and began edging up late that year, before the new tariffs were introduced.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Some of the early upturn predates tariffs, a caveat to full attribution.
insights.quote: began to edge up late that year, before the new tariffs were introduced
insights.locator: The 2025-26 Tariffs and Consumer Goods Prices

insights.claim: The estimates are cross-sectional (more vs. less tariff-exposed non-oil goods, 67 categories) and exclude services, about two-thirds of the consumer basket; tariffs may also shift economy-wide factors in ways that amplify or offset the estimated pressures.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: The figures are partial-equilibrium and goods-only, so macro offsets or amplification through the exchange rate, demand or policy are not captured.
insights.quote: Tariffs may also affect these economy-wide factors in ways that amplify or offset the price pressures we estimate.
insights.locator: The 2025-26 Tariffs and Consumer Goods Prices

themes.theme: Forecast: level stays high, inflation fades

insights.claim: The tariff effect on the consumer goods price level peaked near 3 percent in February 2026 and is forecast to ease to about 2 percent by August 2026, after a Supreme Court ruling ended emergency-powers tariffs and a lower 10 percent surcharge replaced them.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: The legal rollback only partly reverses the price level; about two-thirds of the peak effect remains.
insights.quote: the tariff effect on the consumer goods price level peaked near 3 percent in February 2026
insights.locator: The Tariff Effect on Consumer Goods Inflation Has Peaked

insights.claim: The tariff contribution to twelve-month goods inflation is forecast to fall to around zero by August 2026, turn negative as the large 2025 increases drop out of the comparison, then turn slightly positive by mid-2027 as Canadian tariffs pass through.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Tariffs shift from a goods-inflation tailwind to a modest drag then slight tailwind in 2027, a base-effect disinflation not driven by price declines.
insights.quote: tariffs have left consumer goods price levels higher, while their effect on inflation fades
insights.locator: The Tariff Effect on Consumer Goods Inflation Has Peaked

insights.claim: After August 2026 the tariff effect on the price level edges up again: about half from tariff changes already in place (mainly August 2026 tariffs on Canadian goods still passing through) and the rest from the Canadian auto tariff increase announced for January 2027.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
entities: Canadian cars, trucks, and auto parts
insights.so_what: Canadian-directed tariffs are the live source of renewed goods price pressure, especially autos in early 2027.
insights.quote: the August 2026 tariffs on Canadian goods
insights.locator: The Tariff Effect on Consumer Goods Inflation Has Peaked

insights.claim: The forecast assumes tariffs stay at end-September 2026 levels except the announced January 2027 Canadian auto increase, so any new tariff action would change the path.
insights.speaker: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
insights.so_what: Treat the fading-inflation path as a baseline conditional on no new tariff policy.
insights.locator: The Tariff Effect on Consumer Goods Inflation Has Peaked

source_meta.author: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
